content: Chickenpox, also known as varicella, is a highly contagious infectious disease caused by the varicella-zoster virus (VZV), a member of the herpesvirus family. It is most commonly seen in children and is characterized by the development of numerous itchy, fluid-filled blisters that eventually burst and form crusts. The same virus is responsible for causing shingles (herpes zoster) in adults. Chickenpox does not show any racial or gender predilection, and treatment is typically symptomatic, except in immunocompromised individuals. The disease was first described by the Iranian physician Razi, with further detailed descriptions provided by Giovanni Filippo in the mid-1500s. In 1767, William Heberden differentiated chickenpox from smallpox. The live attenuated vaccine for chickenpox was introduced in 1974. Chickenpox is transmitted through inhalation of aerosolized droplets from nasopharyngeal secretions or direct contact with the vesicular fluid of an infected individual. The virus initially replicates in the regional lymph nodes of the upper respiratory tract, leading to viremia. This viremia results in the widespread invasion of capillary endothelial cells and the epidermis, producing the characteristic vesicular lesions. The infection of the malpighian layer of the skin leads to both intercellular and intracellular edema, forming the hallmark vesicles. The varicella-zoster virus, also known as human herpesvirus 3 (HHV-3), is the causative agent of chickenpox. Transmission occurs via respiratory droplets or direct contact with the vesicular fluid of skin lesions. Chickenpox can be confused with other rash-like conditions, making differential diagnosis essential. However, smallpox is the primary condition that must be ruled out when diagnosing chickenpox. Chickenpox is endemic and primarily spreads through respiratory routes. While cases can occur year-round, they are more common in winter and early spring. In tropical regions, adults are more frequently affected than children. Risk factors for contracting chickenpox include a lack of prior infection or vaccination, being a newborn (especially premature infants or those born to mothers without prior chickenpox infection), immunocompromised individuals, cancer patients, and those on immunosuppressive therapy. Routine screening for chickenpox is not recommended for the general population, as most adults have been exposed to the virus during childhood or have been vaccinated. However, screening is advised for specific groups, including healthcare workers, pregnant women, newborns, individuals with HIV/AIDS, and those undergoing organ transplantation. If left untreated, chickenpox can lead to complications such as bacterial skin infections (e.g., cellulitis) due to scratching, or pneumonia, which can be fatal in some cases. Pregnant women and immunocompromised individuals are at higher risk of severe complications. Pregnant women who are not immune and are exposed to chickenpox may require urgent treatment, as the virus can cause significant harm to the fetus, particularly before 20 weeks of gestation. Individuals who recover from chickenpox remain at risk of developing shingles later in life. The clinical presentation of chickenpox includes a characteristic rash and systemic symptoms. The rash typically begins on the head and trunk before spreading to other parts of the body. It is intensely pruritic and accompanied by systemic symptoms such as low-grade fever, headache, malaise, anorexia, cough, and coryza. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on the appearance of the rash in crops. Laboratory tests, such as Tzanck smears, direct fluorescent antibody testing, or PCR, may be used in atypical cases or for confirmation. Blood tests can detect acute infection (IgM) or past infection and immunity (IgG). Prenatal diagnosis of fetal varicella infection can be performed using ultrasound or PCR testing of amniotic fluid, though these procedures carry risks. Imaging studies, such as chest X-rays, may be used to identify complications like varicella pneumonia, which is rare in children but occurs in approximately 20% of adults. CT scans, MRIs, and ultrasounds have limited diagnostic value for chickenpox unless complications arise. Treatment for chickenpox in otherwise healthy individuals is primarily symptomatic, aimed at relieving discomfort. Antiviral therapy may be considered in high-risk individuals. Surgical intervention is not indicated for chickenpox. Primary prevention involves vaccination, with two doses of the varicella vaccine recommended for children at 12-15 months and 4-6 years of age. Adults who have not been vaccinated or previously infected should receive two doses, spaced at least 28 days apart. Calamine lotion and colloidal oatmeal baths can help reduce itching, while keeping fingernails trimmed short can minimize the risk of skin infections caused by scratching.
